newsitem.title: USA: Enron, Portland merger depends on rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Enron, Portland merger depends on rate cut.

text.p: Enron Corp, after a hearing today before the Oregon Public Utility Commission, said it will need to prove more savings for ratepayers before its planned merger with Portland General Corp will be accepted by the state.
Enron chief executive officer Kenneth Lay said in a conference call with reporters the commission "clearly feels that $3 million (in annual) savings is not enough for a transaction of this size."
Houston-based Enron and Portland General announced last July plans to merger via a tax-free stock-for-stock deal valued near $2.1 billion.
Lay noted the companies have always said "any and all cost savings resulting from the merger would be passed on to consumers."
So far, however, Enron and Portland have estimated those savings at around $3 million per year, compared with much higher calculations by the staff of the Oregon commission.

Late last month the Oregon Public Utility Commission (OPUC) staff approved the merger, but with several conditions, including an annual rate cut of $47.4 million for the first four years after the deal goes through.

The amount was based on factors including savings from the combination of Enron and Portland General's trading operations and compensation for revenues that would have come from the utility's wholesale operations, staff sources said earlier.
The commission on Friday asked the two sides to come up with clear principles regarding the division of the utility's regulated and unregulated businesses, Lay noted.
The OPUC did not address the specifics of costs savings, but instructed the two sides to resume settlement talks.
A settlement conference will likely be scheduled within a few days, Lay said.

He stressed the combination of the natural gas giant with the Northwest utility "is not the typical merger of neighboring utilities" where savings would be generated by eliminating overlapping operations, but said the companies agreed to be more aggressive in identifying savings.
Ken Harrison, chief executive officer of Portland General, said there were still some areas where the commission was unclear, including the issue of wholesale trading revenues.
The OPUC had planned to issue a final decision on the merger on or about March 17.
Lay said the results of Friday's hearing "could delay that a little bit, but we will just have to wait and see."
